title: Giri, Firouzja Advance To Final Match
summary:
GMs Alireza Firouzja and Anish Giri won their matches to advance to the Knockout 1 Final in the Total Chess World Championship Tour Pilot 2026. GM Fabiano Caruana won the second set against Firouzja (including a fast classical win), but the French number-one won the match in armageddon. Giri, on the other hand, won the second set against GM Maxime Vachier-Lagrave—in addition to the first—and avoided the tiebreak altogether.

Day nine starts on Thursday, November 19, at 9 a.m. ET / 15:00 CET / 7:30 p.m. IST.

Knockout 1: Smooth Sailing For Giri, Firouzja Edges Out Caruana

Knockout 2: Niemann, Duda In Final

Knockout 3: Arjun, Martirosyan In Final

Knockout 4: Aronian, So In Final

Knockout 5: Carlsen, Artemiev In Final

Knockout 6: Praggnanandhaa, Mishra In Final

Day two of the Knockout concluded the first set of matches, producing a Final and a Consolation Match in every bracket. As mentioned earlier, the slate was wiped clean and the players again contested four blitz games (3+2), two rapid games (15+10), and one fast classic game (45+30).

The winner earned one "set point" per day, regardless of the margin of their victory, and two set points won the match. In the event of a 1-1 tie—as in Firouzja vs. Caruana, where Firouzja won day one and Caruana won day two—an armageddon game settled the score.

Firouzja wins in armageddon. Photo: Michal Walusza/Total Chess.

Keep reading, but you can also check out GM Hikaru Nakamura's recap video below.

Knockout 1: Smooth Sailing For Giri, Firouzja Edges Out Caruana

The two players who led after Tuesday won their respective matches on Wednesday. For Giri, the road was less complicated; he won both sets without a single loss. On the second day, he won one blitz game and one rapid game, while making draws in all the others.

After the match, he said: "Maxime is obviously a much better player in this type of format, in rapid and blitz, quick chess. I was quite fortunate, played well for my standards, and managed to overcome." As for the Final, he said, "Maybe I'll get lucky!"

Maxime is obviously a much better player in this type of format.

—Anish Giri

Giri interviewed after the game. Photo: Michal Walusza/Total Chess.

Giri held his own in the blitz portion, winning game three. With the black pieces in the Reti Opening, he neutralized an aggressive attempt with 7.Ne5, reached an equal endgame, and capitalized at once on the opportunity to double his opponent's pawns. Vachier-Lagrave must have underestimated the simple-looking 21...Bxc3!, after which the engine claims White is strategically lost.

With set one in the pocket and a point ahead, "don't lose" was the name of the game. And Giri did just that. He was on the better side of a draw in the first rapid game, and then picked up four points in the second rapid game, with the white pieces. The opening didn't go well for Vachier-Lagrave, as he gave Giri the best possible version of a thematic pawn sacrifice in the Queen's Indian Defense. It's not even "just compensation" in this case—White won his pawn back pretty quickly.

Giri confessed that taking a draw with a better position in the fast classic game was a "sin," but it did win him the match. Perhaps he can be forgiven.

As for the other match, there was just one draw in Firouzja vs. Caruana. Firouzja won the first three blitz games but lost the fourth; then, they made a draw and Caruana won a rapid game. In a must-win fast classic game with the black pieces, Firouzja self-destructed and lost the set.

Both players won a set, and it was Firouzja who won the armageddon tiebreak.

Firouzja nearly managed to repeat the 4-0 sweep in blitz, but fell one game short. The three points he earned in blitz, however, were negated by Caruana's one win in rapid, which is worth four points. After the match, Firouzja said that the only thing he'd change about the format is the value of blitz games.

Speaking about the points system as well, GM Nodirbek Abdusattorov (in the sixth bracket) felt that four points for a rapid game was too much.

"I think everything other than the blitz point system is good, but on the blitz point system it's really not fair that I won three games and after I lose one game in rapid you're down in the match." - Alireza Firouzja after winning the match in armageddon https://t.co/ameE5L3Z5k

— chess24 (@chess24com) November 18, 2026

The rapid portion started with a Classical Sicilian (Caruana with White), but the queens got traded and we saw an accurate draw, 98 accuracy by both sides. Game two, an Exchange French, was decisive. With Black in the time scramble, Caruana used his two-minute time advantage (Firouzja on 16 seconds) to find the winning counterblow 38...Rc2!.

After that, Caruana won convincingly in the fast classic game, where Firouzja played the unusual 2...Qa5 against the Alapin Sicilian to generate winning chances. With this win, Caruana has a 2794 classical rating—seven points under Carlsen. GM Rafael Leitao analyzes the Game of the Day.

The match was even at 1-1 after this game, and Firouzja won the armageddon. Caruana lost his a-pawn and the position collapsed—or, in GM David Howell's words, "The black position is cooked."

In David Howell's grandmaster opinion, if Caruana doesn't find a way to stop Bxb7 and a6-a7, "the black position is cooked"! https://t.co/HEJcaXJn6m #TotalChess https://t.co/zed3rT78RG

— chess24 (@chess24com) November 18, 2026

Giri will face Firouzja in the Final, while Caruana and Vachier-Lagrave will contest third place.

Knockout 2: Niemann, Duda In Final

In the second knockout bracket, GM Hans Niemann and GM Jan-Krzysztof Duda defeated GMs Liem Le and Ian Nepomniachtchi. Niemann won both sets, while Duda won a nailbiter armageddon game.

Niemann convincingly defeated the former world number-14. Photo: Michal Walusza/Total Chess.

Niemann won convincingly, with one win and two losses in blitz, a win in rapid, and finally a win in fast classic. Ahead of the final game, with a three-point lead, he had one goal: "Not losing."

Q: "Anything specific you want to focus on going into the classical game?" Hans: "Not losing." #TotalChess https://t.co/3OmBq8IBDU

— chess24 (@chess24com) November 18, 2026

He equalized comfortably in a Closed Catalan and went on to win when Le overpressed. The rook coming down on the c-file made greater threats than its counterpart on the a-file.

After losing the first set on Tuesday, Duda came back from behind to turn the match around. He won the second set with two wins and a loss in blitz, a trade of wins in rapid, and finally a win in fast classic. With a 1-1 score, it was a thriller armageddon that won the Polish grandmaster the match.

Nepomniachtchi had a seven-to-two-minute time advantage, with no increment for another 17 moves. At precisely this moment, WIM Fiona Steil-Antoni foreshadowed, "It feels like unless Ian Nepomniachtchi blunders something big, this is going to be such an uphill battle against the clock," one breath before Nepomniachtchi hung a pawn.

Duda wins an extremely close fight. Photo: Michal Walusza/Total Chess.

The game went downhill from there, but Duda still had to win the game with seconds on the clock. He managed to reach move 41 and play on the increment, but barely. Duda called it "a lucky game," saying that he would have lost if the increment had started after move 60 instead.

The video of the game is more appropriate for the drama than game annotations.

Duda wins an incredibly nervous game on the increment and advances to the Knockout 2 Final against Hans Niemann! #TotalChess https://t.co/J5ItlxIeQ3

— chess24 (@chess24com) November 18, 2026

Nepomniachtchi and Le will still return on Thursday to contest the consolation match.

Knockout 3: Arjun, Martirosyan In Final

In the third bracket, GM Arjun Erigaisi beat GM Jorden van Foreest in armageddon, while GM Haik Martirosyan beat GM Richard Rapport 2-0.

Rapport was one of three players not to show up to the fast classic game, along with GMs Magnus Carlsen (again) and Abhimanyu Mishra. In each case, it did not change the outcome of the match; Rapport would have lost anyway, while Carlsen and Mishra won their matches with a game to spare.

It may be easier for the winner of the match to say, but Martirosyan commented that he would probably never skip a game. "I thought it's good to play chess anyway," he said. "I'm very happy when I am next to the chessboard, but maybe one day if I will be so tired—but I don't think I will do it." He was also full of praise for Rapport: "I played such an interesting, such a fantastic player... I was enjoying [it] because of my opponent's style."

I thought it's good to play chess anyway.

—Haik Martirosyan

Rapport doesn't show up. Photo: Michal Walusza/Total Chess.

Knockout 4: Aronian, So In Final

GMs Levon Aronian and Wesley So have set up an all-American Final in the fourth bracket.

At the start of the day, So entered the confessional booth to publicly apologize for his negative statements about the tournament and its format. He brought notes for the apology, which started with, "I think I was wrong." You can listen to the rest of it in the post below.

Wesley So: "I think I was wrong. I would like to take this time to sincerely apologize for the way I criticized the Total Chess tournament and its format." "I think I was out of place and I should really just stop b****ing." #TotalChess https://t.co/GCQtiJdQ5B

— chess24 (@chess24com) November 18, 2026

Knockout 5: Carlsen, Artemiev In Final

Carlsen and GM Vladislav Artemiev are in the Final. As stated above, Carlsen didn't show up to this game either, and a draw would have sent him under the 2800 rating for the first time in 17 years. He had already clinched his match against GM Bibisara Assaubayeva.

It remains a question: will we see him play a fast classic game against Artemiev?

Carlsen not at the board. Photo: Maria Emelianova/Total Chess.

Knockout 6: Praggnanandhaa, Mishra In Final

GMs Praggnanandhaa Rameshbabu and Mishra are through to the Final. In a funny twist, Praggnanandhaa quipped he was more relieved to avoid playing his sister than he was to win the match. Had he lost against Abdusattorov, he would have played the Consolation Match against GM Vaishali Rameshbabu.

After skipping the fast classic game and winning anyway, Mishra addressed criticism by the CEO of FIDE Enterprises, GM Emil Sutovsky, in an X post. He explained that he was exhausted after seven games a day and that he also received permission from the chief arbiter not to show up to the game. He added that he was still unclear on whether the games would be classically rated or not, if the match was already won.

"Given that uncertainty, combined with the fatigue I felt, plus permission from the chief arbiter, I had sufficient reasons not to show up," he wrote.

Mishra took the option of not showing up. Photo: Maria Emelianova/Total Chess.

With two days left, we are near the end of a long tournament. But one thing's for sure: nobody gets a break! Thursday and Friday feature the last matches, with seven games a day.

How to watch?

You can watch the event on the Chess24 Twitch or YouTube pages, or on GM Hikaru Nakamura's Kick channel. You can find the games on our dedicated events page.

The live broadcast was hosted by GM David Howell, IMs Jovanka Houska and Anna Rudolf, and WIM Fiona Steil-Antoni.

The Total Chess World Championship Tour Pilot 2026 takes place on November 10-21 at the Anantara New York Palace Hotel in Budapest, Hungary. The event is a trial run for the official event in 2027, which will crown the first FIDE World Combined Champion. The event consists of a round-robin group stage and a knockout combining blitz, rapid, and fast classical time controls. The time control is 3+2 for blitz, 15+10 for rapid, 45+30 for fast classical, and 10 minutes (White) vs. 7 minutes (Black) with a one-second increment starting on move 41 in armageddon.

title: Martinez, Oro Lead 9z Globant to 3rd Straight Chess Club Showdown Win
summary:
GM Jose Martinez and the world's youngest GM, Faustino Oro, led the 9z Globant Chess Club to victory in the Chess Club Showdown on November 18. The 72-28 final score marked the team's third straight victory. 9z Globant has now won every showdown since the event debuted in September.

In the Chess Club Showdown, players from every team compete in a two-hour blitz arena. Afterward, the 50 highest-rated players from each of the top two teams compete in a head-to-head finals. The arena features battles between players of every level and rewards winning quickly. This format encourages risky play, as top players try to make quick work of their amateur opponents. In one of his first games, Oro tried a dubious gambit against an opponent rated nearly 3000 points below him.

Martinez earned the top individual spot in the arena, playing dominant chess, while reclining on pillows.

This is what chess excellence looks like.

Like Oro, Martinez sometimes tried creative openings. It worked well overall, but nearly cost him a game, playing down 2500 points.

Behind Martinez's dominant performance, his teammates GM Dmitrij Kollars, GM Jose Carlos Ibarra Jerez, and IM Yoseph Theolifus Taher took the next three spots in the individual standings.

The top 10 individual finishers in the arena.

9z Globant dominated the arena from start to finish, but there was a tight battle for second place and a spot in the finals. Team Liquid played without GMs Magnus Carlsen, Fabiano Caruana, and Praggnanandhaa Rameshbabu, who were all competing in the Total Chess World Championship. Despite their absences, Team Liquid held off their competitors for second place, edging out Natus Vincere, FUT Esports, and Team Vitality, who all scored over 2000 points, claiming third through fifth place in the arena.

9z Globant and Team Liquid earned spots in the finals.

9z and Team Liquid played each other in the finals, as they did the previous two months. While Team Liquid showed impressive depth to take second place in the arena without their stars, they would have greatly benefited from having them in the final match. With a 200+ point rating edge on every board, 9z Globant made quick work of their opponents. Martinez finished in just a couple of minutes. He won his first game in 22 moves, and then his FM opponent resigned immediately in the second game.

Despite their missing stars, Team Liquid actually improved on their score from last month. The 72-28 final score was closer than the 79-21 match in October.

The Chess Club Showdown will return on Wednesday, December 23.

title: Pranav Venkatesh Signs With Revenant XSpark As Indian Esports Teams Add Chess Stars
summary:
GM Pranav Venkatesh has signed with Revenant XSpark as its first chess player, becoming the latest Indian grandmaster to join an esports organization.

The contract comes shortly after the 20-year-old was crowned world junior blitz champion, and he will now represent the Mumbai-based team at the upcoming Google Play Arena in December.

"I'm really happy to be representing Revenant XSpark at Google Play Arena. Chess has been a big part of my life since I was very young, and this is an exciting opportunity to experience a different competitive environment," Pranav said.

"It's also nice to see chess being included alongside other gaming titles, as it gives the game an opportunity to reach people who might not usually follow chess tournaments. I'm looking forward to giving my best and hopefully seeing more young people take an interest in chess."

It's also nice to see chess being included alongside other gaming titles, as it gives the game an opportunity to reach people who might not usually follow chess tournaments.

—Pranav Venkatesh

Welcome, World Junior Chess Champion, Pranav V to Revenant XSpark 💜⚡️ #WolvenSpark #RNTX https://t.co/tGolplSpZV

— Revenant Esports (@RevenantGGWP) November 16, 2026

Pranav, who turned 20 in October, joins Revenant XSpark after winning the FIDE World Junior Blitz Championship in Al Ain, United Arab Emirates, earlier this month. He scored 10.5/13 to finish a full point clear of the field and also took silver in the rapid championship. The blitz gold adds to his 2025 World Junior Championship title.

Rated 2679, he is ranked third in the world among juniors, 42nd overall, and has established himself as one of India's rising generation of young grandmasters.

Pranav has also been in action this past week, helping India win the silver medal at the Asian Nations Cup, scoring 6/9 on board two.

Pranav at the 2025 FIDE World Rapid & Blitz Championship. Photo: Anna Shtourman/FIDE.

Revenant XSpark founder and CEO Rohit Jagasia said:

"Pranav is an exceptional talent, and winning two world titles speaks volumes about his dedication and competitive mindset. Having him represent us as our first chess player at Google Play Arena is a proud moment for Revenant XSpark. With chess establishing itself on major global esports stages, we're excited to bring a player of his caliber into the competitive gaming ecosystem."

Pranav is an exceptional talent, and winning two world titles speaks volumes about his dedication and competitive mindset.

—Rohit Jagasia, CEO Revenant XSpark

Revenant XSpark's move into chess follows a wave of signings that accelerated ahead of the first 2025 Esports World Cup. Among the Indian players to secure deals that year were GM Arjun Erigaisi with Gen.G, GMs Nihal Sarin and Aravindh Chithambaram with S8UL, and GM Praggnanandhaa Rameshbabu with Team Liquid.

The signings have continued in 2026. In April, GMs Faustino Oro (9zGlobant), Sina Movahed (Team Stallions), Pranesh M (S8UL), and Hans Niemann (GodLike Esports) were all picked up by esports organizations.

Checkmate. ♟️ The world chess prodigy Sina Movahed has officially joined Team Stallions! Welcome to the family. 🧡 #WeAreStallions https://t.co/y4t4P1I1I2

— Team Stallions🐎 (@TeamStallionsgg) April 30, 2026

In July, GM Anish Giri joined BASILISK, alongside GM Vincent Keymer. In August, the organization added IM Levy Rozman, better known as GothamChess, as its Head of Chess.

The most recent high-profile signing in the chess world, besides Pranav, came on November 9, when Team Apex Gaming signed two-time Olympiad gold medalist GM Vidit Gujrathi.

🔥🔥🔥 Happy to be part of @Team_ApexGaming Let’s kill it 💪

— Vidit Gujrathi (@viditchess) November 9, 2026

For Pranav and his new team, the immediate focus is Google Play Arena, a new Indian gaming championship launched by Google Play and NODWIN Gaming. The $440,000 tournament features a chess event on Chess.com alongside BGMI, Free Fire MAX, MOBA Legends: 5v5!, Real Cricket, and EA SPORTS FC Mobile.

Beyond the Indian competition, chess was confirmed on November 6 for a third consecutive appearance at the 2027 Esports World Cup. GM Magnus Carlsen, who represents Team Liquid, has won both editions so far.

For a chess player, signing with an esports organization provides a professional team to represent, with deals that can include a six-figure salary, content partnerships, and promotion to new audiences. In return, organizations gain a player who can attract fans and compete under their banner.

At the Esports World Cup, that partnership also has a clear competitive purpose: Players earn points toward their organization's overall Club Championship standing across multiple games. GM Denis Lazavik's runner-up finish in 2026 contributed 750 points to All Gamers, helping the organization win the $7 million club title.

title: Anish Giri and Alireza Firouzja reach Total Chess Final
summary: Aronian and Artemiev win Armageddon tiebreaks as the six bracket finals take shape Anish Giri and Alireza Firouzja secured their places in the final of the Total Chess World Championship Tour Pilot in Budapest on Wednesday. Giri won the second day of his semifinal against Maxime Vachier-Lagrave by 12.5 points to 7.5. Fabiano Caruana won his Fast Classic game against Firouzja to take their second day 15–5 and force a tiebreak, but Firouzja then won a dramatic Armageddon game as Caruana ran out of time. Giri had won Tuesday’s match 14.5–5.5, while Firouzja took the first day against Caruana 12–8. Giri’s second daily victory and Firouzja’s Armageddon win set up their championship final on Thursday and Friday. Vachier-Lagrave and Caruana will meet in the match for third place. Each knockout day has seven games: four Blitz games, two Rapid games and one Fast Classic. A Blitz win is worth one point, a Rapid win four and a Fast Classic win eight, with half for a draw. The scores reset overnight, and a player advances by winning both days or winning one and drawing the other. One win apiece, or two tied days, leads to Armageddon. In the other brackets, Levon Aronian and Vladislav Artemiev won their Armageddon games with Black to secure places in their respective finals. Aronian will face Wesley So for 13th place, while Artemiev will meet Magnus Carlsen for 17th place. Giri stays unbeaten to reach the final Giri again edged the four blitz games 2.5–1.5 against Vachier-Lagrave, winning the third game with Black. After a draw in the first rapid game, he won the second with White to take a lead into Fast Classic. A draw with Black was enough to give him the day 12.5–7.5 and complete his semifinal victory. Giri remained unbeaten across all fourteen games of the match. Caruana’s Fast Classic win forces Armageddon Firouzja won the first three blitz games, extending his winning streak against Caruana in the format, before Caruana took the fourth with Black. A draw and another Black win in rapid put Caruana ahead 7–5. He then won the Fast Classic game with White, adding eight points to take the day 15–5 and level the match at one daily win each. Caruana’s higher two-day point total gave him the choice of colour for Armageddon, and he chose Black. Playing White in Armageddon, Firouzja needed a win to advance. Caruana ran out of time after Firouzja’s 44th move, giving Firouzja the victory and the remaining place in the championship final. Every player still in action Magnus Carlsen swept the four blitz games against Bibisara Assaubayeva and added a win and a draw in rapid to lead 10–2 in the bracket for places 17 to 20. Having already secured qualification, Carlsen forfeited the Fast Classic game, leaving the day tied 10–10. His victory on Tuesday was enough to send him through. He will meet Vladislav Artemiev, who won his Armageddon game with Black against Andrew Hong. Levon Aronian reversed first-day defeat against Shakhriyar Mamedyarov, winning Wednesday’s match 13.5–6.5 before taking Armageddon with Black. He will face Wesley So, who beat Vincent Keymer 13.5–6.5 on the second day. Haik Martirosyan advanced in the bracket for 9th place with an 18–2 day against Richard Rapport, including a Fast Classic win by forfeit. The result of the match was already decided before that game. Hans Moke Niemann also completed two daily wins, beating Le Quang Liem 15.5–4.5 after winning their Fast Classic game with Black. Jan-Krzysztof Duda won Wednesday’s match against Ian Nepomniachtchi 14.5–5.5 to force Armageddon, then won the tiebreak with Black to set up a match against Niemann for fifth place. Day two in the other brackets: Places 5 to 8: Hans Moke Niemann 15.5–4.5 Liem Le; Ian Nepomniachtchi 5.5–14.5 Jan-Krzysztof Duda. Duda won the Armageddon tiebreak. Places 9 to 12: Arjun Erigaisi 8–12 Jorden van Foreest, with Erigaisi winning Armageddon tiebreak; Richard Rapport 2–18 Haik Martirosyan. Places 13 to 16: Levon Aronian 13.5–6.5 Shakhriyar Mamedyarov, with Aronian winning the Armageddon tiebreak; Vincent Keymer 6.5–13.5 Wesley So. Places 17 to 20: Magnus Carlsen 10–10 Bibisara Assaubayeva; Vladislav Artemiev 8–12 Andrew Hong. Artemiev won the Armageddon tiebreak. Places 21 to 24: Praggnanandhaa Rameshbabu 11.5–8.5 Nodirbek Abdusattorov; Vaishali Rameshbabu 9–11 Abhimanyu Mishra. Among the Indian players, Praggnanandhaa Rameshbabu produced a decisive turnaround against Nodirbek Abdusattorov. Trailing 3.5–8.5 before the Fast Classic, he won with Black to take the day 11.5–8.5 and set up a final against Abhimanyu Mishra for 21st place. Arjun Erigaisi’s 8–4 lead became an 8–12 defeat after Jorden van Foreest won Fast Classic, sending their match to Armageddon, which Arjun Erigaisi won with White. Vaishali Rameshbabu received a Fast Classic win by forfeit, but Mishra had already secured the day and advanced with an 11–9 score. The finals and third-place matches in all six brackets are played on Thursday, November 19, and Friday, November 20, with blitz from 15:00 CET, rapid at 16:15 and 17:30 and Fast Classic at 18:45. Armageddon follows on Friday where needed. A total of $650,000 in prize money is at stake across the six brackets. The semifinals have provided the first full test of Total Chess, with Blitz, Rapid and Fast Classic counting in the same match. Testing the format in a live competitive environment is one of the primary objectives of the Budapest pilot, together with seeing how the rules work in practice and evaluating whether certain aspects of the regulations could be refined. Full results: totalchess.com/tournaments/budapest-2026 Text: Total Chess Photos: Maria Emelianova and Michal Walusza Official website: www.totalchess.com About Total Chess Total Chess is a global championship platform established to redefine elite competitive chess for the modern era. Developed by Norway Chess and approved by FIDE, the Total Chess World Championship Tour introduces a unified format that crowns the world’s ultimate champion by testing excellence across three disciplines: Fast Classical, Rapid and Blitz. The Tour will bring together the world’s top 24 men and women players to compete across four premier international events

title: FIDE World Rapid & Blitz Championships 2026: Registration now open
summary: Every December, the chess world comes together for one of its most exciting traditions: crowning four world champions in rapid and blitz chess, in both the open and women’s events. With a world-class lineup, lightning-fast action, and dramatic finishes, the championships keep fans on the edge of their seats from start to finish. Vibrant Istanbul is ready to welcome the elite of chess from 26 to 30 December 2026. The rapid and blitz championships consistently attract the strongest players, drawn by the prestige of the titles, a prize fund of more than €1,000,000, and the unique festive atmosphere of this end-of-year event. Participation is reserved for top-level competitors. Players rated 2550 or higher are eligible for the open events, while a minimum rating of 2250 is required for the women’s competition. Over the years, these titles have been won by some of the biggest names in chess. Magnus Carlsen is the record holder who has claimed nine world blitz titles and six world rapid titles. In the women’s events, Kateryna Lagno has won four titles (one rapid and three blitz), while Bibisara Assaubayeva is a three-time Women’s World Blitz Champion. Among other recent winners are such superstars like Ju Wenjun, Humpy Koneru, Nodirbek Abdusattorov, Vasyl Ivanchuk, Daniil Dubov, and other top grandmasters. The registration for this prestigious event is now open! Below is the key information. Full details can be found in the Regulations, linked at the end of this article. Schedule The arrival day is 25 December, with departures scheduled for 31 December. The World Rapid Championships will be held from 26-28 December, while the World Blitz Championships will take place on 29-30 December. Eligibility Open Section Players rated 2550 or higher in any of the twelve 2026 FIDE rating lists (Standard, Rapid, or Blitz). Women’s Section Players rated 2250 or higher in any of the twelve 2026 FIDE rating lists (Standard, Rapid, or Blitz). Both Sections National Champions of 2026 (Standard, Rapid, or Blitz) representing a FIDE member federation, regardless of title or rating. Please note that players are responsible for submitting their own registrations. Federations cannot register players on their behalf. Accommodation and travel support Players rated 2750 or higher in any of the twelve 2026 FIDE rating lists (Standard, Rapid, or Blitz) are entitled to reimbursement of travel expenses and accommodation in a standard room. For the women’s championships, the rating threshold is 2550. In addition, the gold, silver, and bronze medallists from the 2025 World Rapid and Blitz Championships are entitled to complimentary accommodation too. Entry fees Open Championship €100 if paid by 15 December 2026 €200 if paid after 15 December 2026 Women’s Championship €50 if paid by 15 December 2026 €100 if paid after 15 December 2026 We would like to remind players of the proper conduct: fair play, compliance with the dress code, cooperation with the press, and attendance at the ceremonies and technical meeting. title: Total Chess: Giri and Firouzja to battle for tournament title
summary:
Alireza Firouzja and Anish Giri will face each other in the final of the Total Chess Pilot in Budapest. Giri defeated Maxime Vachier-Lagrave in straight sets, while Firouzja needed an Armageddon decider to overcome Fabiano Caruana. Meanwhile, Magnus Carlsen once again forfeited his final fast classic game, with Richard Rapport and Abhimanyu Mishra following suit. The decisions have prompted further discussion about the tournament's format and demanding schedule. | Photo: Michal Walusza / Total Chess

Firouzja wins Armageddon decider, Giri cruises into Budapest final

Alireza Firouzja and Anish Giri have reached the final of the Total Chess Pilot in Budapest, where they will compete for overall victory in a two-set match on Thursday and Friday. Giri secured a 2–0 victory over Maxime Vachier-Lagrave, while Firouzja needed an Armageddon decider to get past Fabiano Caruana. Wednesday's action also saw three players forfeiting their final fast classic games, including Magnus Carlsen, who repeated his controversial decision from the previous day.

Giri completed a convincing semifinal victory over Maxime Vachier-Lagrave, winning both sets of their encounter. After Tuesday's 14½–5½ success , the Dutchman scored another win in blitz and one in rapid on Wednesday, with all remaining games ending in draws. He thus entered the final fast classic encounter with a 5-point advantage, putting Vachier-Lagrave in a must-win situation.

Giri also obtained an advantage in the final game, but eventually agreed to a draw from a position of strength. He later described that decision as "a sin". The Dutch ace, one of the more outspoken players on the elite circuit, also acknowledged that he had been "quite fortunate" to beat MVL in both blitz and rapid chess on both days, as he considers the Frenchman an overall stronger player in the faster formats.

Anish Giri giving an interview | Photo: Michal Walusza

The other semifinal was considerably more closely contested. Firouzja had won Tuesday's opening set against Caruana, meaning that a draw or better on Wednesday would have been enough to advance. The Frenchman started well, winning three of the four blitz games, with Caruana taking the remaining encounter. However, the American turned the tables in the rapid section, scoring a win and a draw to move ahead on the scoreboard.

Firouzja once again questioned the tournament's scoring system, arguing that giving rapid victories four times the value of blitz wins was not an ideal arrangement. Having lost his advantage, he needed to win the fast classic encounter to avoid an Armageddon decider. Instead, he misplayed the black side of a Sicilian Alapin and lost to Caruana.

It was a tough match between two of the strongest players in the world - Alireza Firouzja and Fabiano Caruana | Photo: Michal Walusza

It was Caruana's fifth victory in twelve fast classic games in Budapest, a format that counts towards the official classical ratings. The result took him back to second place in the live rankings with 2794.2 points, exactly 7 behind Magnus Carlsen . With two more fast classic games remaining for both players, the American still has a chance to end the tournament as world number one.

Caruana's victory in the final game gave him a 15–5 win in Wednesday's set, levelling the semifinal at one set apiece and forcing Armageddon. Having scored more points across the two sets, Caruana earned the right to choose his colour and opted for Black, with draw odds.

Firouzja, however, quickly gained a pawn from the white side of an Italian Opening and went on to convert his advantage without major difficulties. The 44-move victory secured his place in the final against Giri, despite having lost Wednesday's set by a wide margin.

A smiling Alireza Firouzja speaking with the press | Photo: Michal Walusza

Knockouts 2-6

Hans Niemann and Jan-Krzysztof Duda will compete for fifth place after winning their respective semifinals. Niemann had little trouble against Le Quang Liem, completing a 2–0 set victory with scores of 13½–6½ and 15½–4½. The 23-year-old Californian won both fast classic games against his Vietnamese opponent and has now scored 8/12 in that format. His results have earned him 14.2 rating points, taking him back above the 2700 mark .

Duda's route to the next stage was considerably more complicated. After losing Tuesday's opening set against Ian Nepomniachtchi, the Polish grandmaster took a one-point lead in Wednesday's blitz section. The two players then exchanged rapid victories, leaving Nepomniachtchi needing a win in the fast classic game to avoid the possibility of a decider. Instead, Duda won that encounter, forcing Armageddon.

Unlike Caruana in the title bracket, Nepomniachtchi chose to play white in the sudden-death game. Duda obtained a clear advantage, but found himself running seriously short of time against an opponent known for his speed in rapid and blitz chess. Despite having to rely on the one-second increment, the Polish star managed to convert his advantage. He later described his victory as "lucky", given how little time he had left on the clock.

Hans Niemann is having a good tournament in Budapest | Photo: Michal Walusza

Ian Nepomniachtchi and Jan-Krzysztof Duda, two formidable GMs, played a hard-fought match | Photo: Michal Walusza

The remaining four brackets also produced their finalists:

Ninth place: Arjun Erigaisi defeated Jorden van Foreest in Armageddon and will face Haik Martirosyan, who beat Richard Rapport by 2–0 in sets.

Thirteenth place: Levon Aronian needed Armageddon to overcome Shakhriyar Mamedyarov and will meet Wesley So, who defeated Vincent Keymer 2–0.

Seventeenth place: Vladislav Artemiev advanced past Andrew Hong in Armageddon and will meet Magnus Carlsen, who defeated Bibisara Assaubayeva by 1½–½ in sets.

Twenty-first place: Praggnanandhaa Rameshbabu beat Nodirbek Abdusattorov 2–0 in an all-elite encounter and will face Abhimanyu Mishra, who also won both sets against Vaishali Rameshbabu.

Two top ten players who are having a great year but did not perform as expected in the group stage - Praggnanandhaa Rameshbabu and Nodirbek Abdusattorov | Photo: Michal Walusza

Three more forfeits raise questions

Following the controversy surrounding Carlsen's decision not to play his final fast classic game against Assaubayeva on Tuesday , the Norwegian once again declined to appear for the last encounter on Wednesday. By that point, he had won all four blitz games, followed by a win and a draw in rapid, giving him a 10–2 lead. Since the final game was worth 8 points, a forfeit loss would leave the set tied at 10–10, enough for Carlsen to advance.

This time, however, he was not the only player to skip the final game. Richard Rapport, who had already lost his match against Haik Martirosyan, also failed to appear, as did Abhimanyu Mishra, who had secured victory against Vaishali before their fast classic encounter.

The fact that two other players followed Carlsen's example might reduce some of the criticism directed at the Norwegian, although the situation has also raised broader questions about the tournament's format and the obligation to play games once a match has been decided.

Bibisara Assaubayeva got to play eight blitz games and four rapid games against the best player in the world | Photo: Michal Walusza

Emil Sutovsky, who had strongly criticised Carlsen's decision on Tuesday, again expressed his disapproval. In a social media post , he argued that the leading figures in chess have a responsibility towards the sport's development. He noted that an ambitious project such as Total Chess depends on satisfying investors, sponsors and broadcasters, and questioned whether television networks would remain interested if important games were regularly left unplayed. In his view, growing chess requires a collective effort from all major stakeholders.

Mishra responded directly to Sutovsky, offering a different perspective . The 17-year-old first praised the organisers and described the tournament as an excellent initiative, but pointed out that the schedule had been particularly demanding, with seven games played each day during the knockout stage. Mishra also pointed to the uncertainty surrounding the rating status of games played after a match had already been decided.

The episode has added another question for the organisers to consider ahead of the full Total Chess Tour in 2027, particularly regarding the combination of a demanding daily schedule, officially rated fast classic games and matches that can be decided before the final encounter.

title: Total Chess: Firouzja and Giri win opening sets, Carlsen sparks controversy
summary:
Alireza Firouzja and Anish Giri (pictured) won the opening sets of their semifinal matches at the Total Chess Pilot in Budapest, defeating Fabiano Caruana and Maxime Vachier-Lagrave respectively. The first day of knockout action also brought controversy, as Magnus Carlsen declined to play the final fast classic game against Bibisara Assaubayeva, having already secured the set victory. The Norwegian's decision prompted criticism, given the game's implications for his classical rating. | Photo: Michal Walusza / Total Chess

Scoring system comes under scrutiny

The knockout stage of the Total Chess Pilot began in Budapest on Tuesday, with Alireza Firouzja and Anish Giri winning the opening sets of their semifinal matches against Fabiano Caruana and Maxime Vachier-Lagrave, respectively. The day also saw Magnus Carlsen attract attention for a different reason: having already secured victory against Bibisara Assaubayeva, the Norwegian decided not to play the final fast classic game, which he lost by forfeit.

Following Monday's rest day, all 24 participants returned to action. The tournament's unusual format keeps every player in contention, although only the four group winners can still compete for the overall title. The remaining participants are divided into five additional knockout brackets, according to their finishing positions in the group stage . The six brackets, each featuring four players, will determine the final standings, with the second-placed players competing for fifth place, the third-placed players for ninth place, and so on.

Each knockout match consists of two sets, played on consecutive days. A set features four blitz games, worth 1 point per win; two rapid games, worth 4 points per win; and one fast classic game, worth 8 points per win. The scores reset after each day, meaning that winning the first set by a large margin provides no advantage beyond the result itself.

The format has raised a few questions, particularly regarding the order of play. Why begin with blitz rather than the longer time control, as is often the case in mixed-format competitions? Should the players not be encouraged to show their best chess in the longest game, rather than reaching it already tired after six faster encounters?

The scoring system is another point of discussion. A rapid victory is worth four times as much as a blitz win, meaning that a player who loses all four blitz games can equalise the score with a single rapid victory. This was precisely what happened in Tuesday's match between Firouzja and Caruana in the main bracket.

It remains to be seen whether the organisers will address these questions ahead of the 2027 Total Chess Tour. After all, the tour will award two of the eight places (i.e. 25 percent) in the Candidates Tournament.

Playing seven games against elite opposition is surely exhausting - Ian Nepomniachtchi v. Jan-Krzysztof Duda and Haik Martirosyan v. Richard Rapport | Photos: Michal Walusza

Firouzja and Giri take the lead

The four group winners are competing for the overall title, with Firouzja facing Caruana and Giri taking on Vachier-Lagrave in the semifinals. Both Firouzja and Giri won their opening sets on Tuesday, though their victories came in rather different circumstances.

Firouzja defeated Caruana by a 12–8 score, making full use of his speed in the blitz section. The Frenchman won all four games to take a 4–0 lead, but saw his advantage disappear immediately when Caruana won the first rapid encounter, worth 4 points.

The American then had good chances to score a second consecutive victory in the following game, which would have given him the lead. However, Firouzja managed to turn things around in a hard-fought encounter, showing his quickness once again during the time-trouble phase. Thus, his ability to handle the faster time controls proved crucial.

With the two players having exchanged rapid victories, the score stood at 8–4 in Firouzja's favour ahead of the fast classic game. A draw in that final encounter left the Frenchman with a 12–8 victory in the opening set.

Alireza Firouzja (winner) v. Fabiano Caruana | Photos: Michal Walusza

Giri's victory over Vachier-Lagrave was more straightforward, despite five of the seven games ending in draws. The Dutchman won one blitz game, while the remaining three blitz encounters and both rapid games were drawn. The decisive result came in the fast classic encounter, in which Vachier-Lagrave was already in a must-win situation.

Giri won that game as well, securing a 14½–5½ victory. Although most of the games ended peacefully, the Dutchman appeared to be in better shape throughout the day.

Neither Caruana nor Vachier-Lagrave is out of contention, however. Under the regulations, winning Wednesday's second set by any margin would force an Armageddon decider. The combined scores of the two sets would only determine the choice of colour in case that sudden-death game takes place.

Maxime Vachier-Lagrave | Photo: Michal Walusza

Knockouts 2-6

In the knockout for fifth place, Hans Niemann and Ian Nepomniachtchi recorded clear victories over Le Quang Liem and Jan-Krzysztof Duda, respectively. Both winners scored with the white pieces in their fast classic encounters, collecting 8 points from the most valuable game of the day.

Hans Niemann | Photo: Michal Walusza

The matches in the bracket for ninth place were more closely contested, with Arjun Erigaisi getting the better of Jorden van Foreest and Haik Martirosyan defeating Richard Rapport.

Elsewhere, Shakhriyar Mamedyarov and Wesley So won their opening sets in the knockout for 13 th place, while Magnus Carlsen and Vladislav Artemiev did the same in the bracket for 17 th place. Praggnanandhaa Rameshbabu and Abhimanyu Mishra were the winners in the knockout for 21 st place.

Jorden van Foreest was defeated by Arjun Erigaisi | Photo: Michal Walusza

Shakhriyar Mamedyarov beat Levon Aronian in the battle of veterans | Photo: Michal Walusza

Carlsen forfeits final game against Assaubayeva

One of Tuesday's main talking points was Carlsen's decision not to play the final fast classic game against Bibisara Assaubayeva. The Norwegian had already secured victory in their opening set, having collected three wins and a draw in blitz, followed by two rapid victories. The score stood at 11½–½, leaving Assaubayeva unable to catch up even with the 8 points available in the final game.

Carlsen, however, had an additional consideration. His difficult group-stage performance had cost him 21.8 classical rating points, leaving him on 2801.2 in the live rankings , just above the 2800 mark. A draw against Assaubayeva would have taken him below 2800 for the first time in 17 years, while a defeat would have left him just 0.7 points ahead of Hikaru Nakamura. A Caruana victory could also have ended his uninterrupted reign as world number one, which began in July 2011.

Bibisara Assaubayeva played six rapid and blitz games against Magnus Carlsen on Tuesday | Photo: Michal Walusza

As it happened, the game was never played. Assaubayeva waited at the board, and after 15 minutes Carlsen was given a forfeit loss. Speaking to Norway's TV 2, the Norwegian explained that the match already decided and believed that, if the final game still had to be played, it should not count towards the ratings.

That position is not unheard of in match situations where the result has already been decided. However, it subsequently became clear that the organisers had informed the players during the pre-event technical meeting that all games would be played and rated.

Total Chess founder Kjell Madland explained that, with the match already decided, Carlsen did not need to play the final game. Madland also stated that no changes had been made to the regulations, implying that other players in the same situation would be able to make the same decision without facing consequences.

Magnus Carlsen | Photo: Michal Walusza

The incident prompted criticism on social media. Emil Sutovsky wrote :

Hard to comment on such a pathetic unsportsmanlike conduct.

Hans Niemann published a longer statement questioning whether the regulations were being applied consistently while bringing back past situations in which he considered that Carlsen had been favoured by organisers:

Whether games could count even after the match was discussed and agreed upon in the technical meeting. If Carlsen was playing someone with a higher rating, he might have been more inclined to play. Nevertheless, if any other player forfeited a game, disrespecting the organiser and his opponent, they would have lost the match by forfeit. It's incredibly disappointing to see continued favouritism towards one player. Let's not forget the jeans, and "Co World Champion" saga. All rules must be applied equally, regardless of the player. End of story.

Wesley So, on the other hand, took a more understanding view of Carlsen's decision, pointing to the rating implications:

He has nothing to gain. If he draws, Hikaru will be very happy! Hikaru's just like a crocodile waiting on the water right now.
